content:
Everyone with arthritis or frailty should be able to understand their condition and get the right help, whatever their language, culture, faith, disability or immigration status. This page sets out how Living With Arthritis plans to make its information more accessible, and the practical rights you have now when using the NHS, such as a free interpreter.

Our aims

Living With Arthritis aims to help people living with arthritis and frailty make informed choices, maintain everyday function and find appropriate professional support. Our education is open to everyone. We want to address barriers experienced by Asian communities, Muslim women, refugees and asylum seekers, and other groups, without assuming everyone has the same needs.

This is a delivery plan, not a claim that every service is already available. Health information on this site is educational and cannot guarantee prevention of joint problems.

First 30 days: listen and make information easier to use

  • invite voluntary feedback about language, disability access, privacy and practical barriers. We will not ask for immigration status or unnecessary medical details.
  • prioritise plain English, readable printouts, captions and accessible page navigation
  • identify trusted community partners and clinical reviewers, and publish only verified qualifications and real review dates

Days 31 to 60: develop culturally appropriate resources

  • plan professionally checked translations based on community demand, starting with Arabic, Urdu and relevant refugee languages
  • co-design resources with Asian communities and Muslim women, covering privacy, modesty, interpreter requests, suitable activity settings and culturally familiar food choices
  • offer information about discussing fasting, medicines and long-term conditions with a clinician, rather than advising people to change treatment themselves
  • provide clear NHS signposting for refugees and asylum seekers, linking to current official guidance rather than promising eligibility for every service

Days 61 to 90: pilot and evaluate

  • pilot accessible education sessions with community partners once staff and safeguarding arrangements are in place
  • focus on individually appropriate strength and balance activity, pacing, falls awareness, nutrition and seeking assessment for persistent symptoms
  • measure accessibility, understanding, usefulness of referrals and participant feedback. We will not claim clinical improvement without suitable evidence.

Your rights when using the NHS now

  • free interpreters: NHS England says patients should be able to have a professional interpreter, including British Sign Language, for GP and hospital appointments. Ask when you book. You should not have to rely on family members, especially children.
  • accessible information: under the Accessible Information Standard, NHS and social care services in England should record and meet your communication needs, such as large print, easy read or a support worker.
  • registering with a GP: you do not need proof of address or immigration status to register with a GP practice in England.
  • a chaperone can be requested for any examination, and you can ask to see a female or male clinician where possible.
  • reasonable adjustments, such as longer appointments, are available for disabled people.

Practical steps for musculoskeletal health

  • speak to a GP or physiotherapist about persistent joint pain, swelling, falls or difficulty with daily tasks
  • ask for activity adapted to your health and ability, particularly if you are frail or at risk of falls. Women-only exercise sessions are available in many areas.
  • discuss medicines, fasting, nutrition and vitamin D with a pharmacist or clinician
  • ask your council for a free needs assessment if you need help at home

These steps support health but cannot prevent every musculoskeletal condition.

Fasting and arthritis medicines

If you fast for religious reasons, talk to your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team well in advance. Some medicines can be taken at different times, and some people may be advised not to fast for health reasons. Never change or stop medicines without advice.

Get involved

We welcome feedback on how accessible our information is. If you work with a community group and would like to partner with us, please get in touch through our contact page.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.
